title: How Software Factories Break Down Work
body:
One of the hardest problems in building a software factory is deciding what the work should be. A large objective arrives in human terms, but agents need something much more concrete. Someone or something has to understand the intent and discover the pieces of work required to achieve it. The system needs to determine which pieces belong together, identify dependencies, decide what can happen in parallel, and keep that understanding current as the work happens.

It is tempting to believe that today’s advanced reasoning models can solve this problem on their own. Today’s models can, in fact, take a large objective, reason about how to approach it, and delegate pieces of the work to subagents. They are already surprisingly good at breaking down work this way.

But a software factory needs more than that. It needs its own intelligence for shaping, tracking, and revising the work around those delegation decisions. This is one of the defining features that separates software factories from agent harnesses.

The system around the model increasingly shapes the work. And that’s why breaking down and delegating work is where some of the most interesting innovation in AI is happening today.

Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Vercel’s eve, OpenAI’s Symphony, Warp, and Factory all break work apart, but they each take different approaches. Let’s explore some of those approaches. At the simpler end, the model creates prompts for subagents. At the more ambitious end, the factory itself becomes an intelligent planning system.

  1. Subagent Delegation

The simplest form of decomposition is direct delegation. A model looks at a large objective, identifies a smaller piece of it, creates a prompt for another agent, and gives that worker enough context to perform the assignment.

If you ask an agent to add enterprise SSO, it might decide that one subagent should investigate the existing authentication system, another should examine the required database changes, and another should work on the frontend. Each worker gets a bounded assignment and usually a separate context.

Claude Code subagents broadly follow this pattern. Codex gives the model primitives for spawning and managing other agents and can recursively delegate, allowing a worker to discover another piece of work and create a child agent for it. Vercel’s Eve similarly lets a parent create isolated child sessions and can require structured results from those workers.

This is already an impressive model capability. The model has to understand the larger objective well enough to invent useful boundaries around the work, and it also has to decide what information each worker needs. Decomposing work and decomposing context are closely related.

But most of the structure still lives in the prompts. The parent may know that one task exists because of a particular requirement or that another cannot begin until some architectural decision is settled, while the system itself has little durable representation of those relationships.

  1. Tracked Tasks

The next step is to turn those inferred pieces of work into task objects that software can coordinate.

Gemini CLI’s task tracker lets the model create tasks and epics, establish dependencies, and update status. Claude Agent Teams gives agents a shared task list with ownership and dependencies. OpenAI’s Symphony can use Codex to generate implementation tasks and dependencies for a larger objective, then persist them in Linear while Symphony dispatches work as it becomes eligible.

This creates a deliberate boundary between model intelligence and conventional software. The model can infer that the API work depends on a schema change, but once that dependency has been discovered there is no reason to ask an LLM repeatedly whether the API task is blocked. A normal scheduler can enforce it.

The task graph itself is not innovative. Neither are IDs, statuses, queues, DAGs, retries, or dependency resolution. We’ve been doing this for decades. The newer capability is producing the graph from an understanding of the objective and the software environment.

Tracked tasks therefore solve an important systems problem, but they still leave the harder question largely untouched: what should shape the decomposition in the first place?

  1. Factory-Shaped Work

Instead of allowing the model to invent every aspect of the process from scratch, the factory can supply a structure for how work should be understood and divided. That structure can encode how the organization actually builds software: the stages work passes through, the roles involved, the policies that apply, the skills available, the approvals required, and the kinds of artifacts that should be produced along the way.

Warp’s factory architecture is a useful example. A factory can define agents around stages such as triage, specification, implementation, and review, along with the models, tools, skills, permissions, and handoffs associated with those stages. The model still has to interpret the incoming work, but it does so inside an opinionated system that already knows something about how this organization expects software to be built.

A generic model with a “spawn agent” tool can invent almost any decomposition it wants. A software factory can instead give the model a vocabulary or schema for good work. For example, it can mandate that some requests be specified before implementation. The vocabulary could also require that some changes produce an architectural decision before code begins or undergo a security review after.

The factory can encode those expectations once and make them part of every future decomposition.

This is one place where the factory contributes real intelligence of its own. The model still supplies semantic understanding, but the decomposition is no longer only a product of the model’s priors and whatever context happened to fit into its window. It is shaped by the organization’s way of working.

  1. Outcome-Linked Work

Even a well-designed factory can break a project into perfectly reasonable tasks and still not achieve the overall goals of the project.

This is one of the deepest problems in decomposition. If a model misunderstands the objective at the beginning, it can create an internally coherent plan, execute every task successfully, and still fail to deliver what the user wanted. Better scheduling does nothing to help because the wrong work is being scheduled perfectly.

Factory’s Missions architecture is interesting because it attacks this problem before implementation begins. The system first develops a validation contract containing behavioral assertions about what should be true when the mission succeeds. Implementation features are then created in relation to those assertions.

Instead of simply asking which tasks sound appropriate, the system can reason about whether its proposed work accounts for the desired outcomes. In principle, if the objective implies eight behaviors and the work graph addresses seven of them, that gap can become visible before or during execution rather than being discovered after every task is marked complete.

The graph it creates as part of this reasoning then represents more than execution order. It represents the relationship between human intent and what the factory is doing about it.

As agents become more autonomous, humans cannot inspect every intermediate decision. The factory needs its own durable representation of why the work being performed is relevant to the original goal.

  1. Dynamic Work Graphs

One of the latest innovations is what to do when the first decomposition is wrong, as it will often be.

Software work is discovery. An agent implementing an API may learn that the real constraint lives in the data model. A migration may expose an undocumented compatibility requirement. Two tasks thought to be independent may collide on the same abstraction. A verification step may reveal an entire category of missing work.

A static task graph handles these discoveries badly. The factory can retry failed work or ask an agent to fix a bug, but the underlying model of the project may itself be wrong.

A dynamic work graph allows the factory to revise its conception of the job. A task can be split after an agent discovers it contains two independent problems. A new dependency can be introduced when workers discover that their assumptions overlap. Downstream work can be invalidated when an upstream interface changes. Entirely new work can appear because validation exposed something the initial planner missed.

Codex’s recursive delegation already offers a simple form of this because workers can discover and create more work during execution. Factory’s validation loop can similarly expose gaps that lead to additional implementation work. Systems with persistent task graphs have the opportunity to make these revisions visible to the whole factory instead of burying them in a single agent’s conversation.

This is one of the more important emerging capabilities in software factories, and it’s still immature. None of these are fully baked yet. Traditional workflow engines are excellent at executing a process someone has already designed. A software factory increasingly has to discover the process while performing it.

The initial work graph is therefore better understood as a hypothesis. The factory proposes one interpretation of how the objective should be accomplished, begins executing it, and uses what its agents learn to improve that interpretation.

Future Research Needed Around the Schema of Work

One area that deserves much more attention is the schema we use to represent work. Most current systems lean too far in one direction or the other. Either the orchestrator owns the work and agents execute what they are given, or the agents own the decomposition and the surrounding system mostly observes what they decide to do.

Neither extreme seems sufficient for a real software factory. The factory needs enough structure to enforce how work should be shaped, tracked, connected to outcomes, and coordinated across many agents. But the agents also need enough freedom to discover that the current plan is wrong, create new work, change dependencies, split tasks, or introduce artifacts and evidence that the factory could not have anticipated ahead of time.

That suggests we need more symmetrical schemas for work. The orchestrator and the agents should be operating on the same underlying model, even if they have different permissions and responsibilities.

The research question is how to connect them in a model that is expressive enough for agents to extend, structured enough for the factory to govern, and durable enough to survive across many workers and many rounds of replanning.

This feels like an important next step for software factories. Running more agents is getting easier, and the infrastructure for scheduling and coordinating them is maturing quickly. The harder problem is creating a shared representation of the work that both the factory and the agents can understand and evolve together.

The software factories that get this right will have more than better orchestration. They will have a better way to turn human intent into work, keep that work aligned with the goal, and revise the plan as reality teaches the system more about the problem.
